Typesense is an open source search engine that can be downloaded and run from your computer locally or from any server.
Typesense combines typo-tolerant keyword search with direct vector search, hybrid search, semantic search, and geo search.

Typesense is more battle-tested in high-scale production environments, and includes automatic Raft leader election in its open-source server, along with type validation, stable JOINs and nested filters, Natural Language Search, and RAG.
It also offers native integrations with LLMs of your choice to enable Natural Language Search and built-in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
Connect your AI agent to Typesense Cloud and it can create and configure clusters, build collections, index your data, tune search and read metrics, all from the conversation.

One commenter called Typesense "A dream come true. Something I've been looking for, for a long time now."
A commenter praised the docs: "The readme and website demonstrate and explain it well."

A Lucene user said Typesense is a very close match to Lucene's feature set plus a REST interface. They were glad to see a solution positioned leaner than Solr/Elastic, which "really are a bit heavy for many occasions."
Criticism: "Bit of a bad look that I can't search the docs using typesense."

A user highlighted memory efficiency: 1 million HN titles with points use 165 MB in Typesense versus 88 MB as JSON on disk. They also liked the compact filter_by and sort_by syntax with qualifiers (e.g. 'publication_year:<1998', 'publication_year:desc').

A user with a ~55 million book dataset worried that keeping everything in memory would be a resource hog on a server. Because the examples use a much smaller subset, they were unsure how well Typesense scales.

An Elasticsearch/Lucene practitioner said Algolia-style engines like this one (presumably) are fast because the whole non-sharded index sits in memory. In their view, that caps it at smallish datasets with loose ranking requirements. It lacks Lucene's tuning knobs, but is fine when search just needs to be low-hassle for non-expert teams.
Positive note on implementation: "It's written in C++, and the code is simple enough to skim. I would expect this to be some hefty Java thing."
Bug report: the homepage demo search box shows "undefined result. Page 1 of NaN" when the query is empty or returns no results.

Feature gaps raised at the time:
- A user wanted index-restricted API keys comparable to Algolia's secured API keys.
- Another hoped for InstantSearch-level UI library support (JS, React, Vue, mobile), calling it one of Algolia's strongest features.

Users asked about language support: non-English languages, accent normalization in typo search, stemming (run/running), and CJK text without whitespace. This suggests these were open questions or concerns for adopters.
Early user feedback: "Love the instant search queries and the fuzzy text matching."
A Rails developer moved from Meilisearch ("which is great") to Elastic for more complex aggregation queries. They planned to try Typesense as a good option for instant-search-like behavior.
A user found OpenSearch a heavy service to run in docker compose for a Rails project. They decided to use Typesense or Meilisearch on their next project as lighter alternatives.
Comparison: a Rails developer who likes the Typesense founder has been using Meilisearch more on client projects over the past year. They cited its "top of the line" Rails integration.
Skepticism about adoption: a user asked who is running Typesense at scale and what the reviews are. Another replied that the lack of answers ("Crickets..") "is all you need to know."
